title: Word Counter
story: Your English teacher assigns a 1000-word essay. How do you count words? By hand? No — build a word counter that handles spaces, tabs, newlines, and punctuation. Then extend it to count sentences and paragraphs too.
why: Word counting teaches state-machine logic: tracking whether you're 'inside a word' as you scan character by character — a fundamental text processing pattern.
analogy: Reading a book, your finger traces each word. When you hit a space, the word ends and a new one begins. Your word counter's `in_word` flag is that finger — it knows when you've left one word and entered another. Sentences are marked by punctuation stop signs (., !, ?).
try_it: Add `average_word_length` (total chars / total words, excluding spaces). Add `most_common_word` that returns the word appearing most frequently. Handle edge cases: multiple spaces, leading/trailing spaces, and empty strings.
tips: The `in_word` flag tracks word boundaries — transitions from space to non-space = new word
Paragraphs are separated by blank lines (consecutive newlines)
common_mistakes: Counting every character as a word — only transitions matter
Forgetting to handle multiple consecutive spaces
Not resetting `in_word` on spaces — leads to undercounting
